title: New routes down the same street
allegory: A tensor is one long street of numbered houses; its strides are the postman's route card (skip 5 doors for the next row, 1 for the next column), and as_strided hands him a new card that visits the same houses in a new pattern without moving a single one.
map: the one long street of numbered houses
the flat storage buffer under every tensor
the route card: skip 5 doors per row, 1 per column
handing the postman a new card
as_strided(x, size, stride): a new view, nothing copied
two legs of the route that both step one door
a sliding-window view: the kernel axis reuses the input's stride
a postman who follows the card and asks nothing
no check against the shape: wrong strides give wrong numbers, silently

chapters.name: The black box
chapters.note: slide a window with no loop and no copy?

cap.1: A convolution slides a small window along the data. Loops are slow, and copying every overlapping window wastes memory. There is a sneakier way.
cap.2: Naive conv1d loops over positions and copies each window, so a number gets copied once for every window it sits in. We want all the windows at once, with zero copies.
cap.3: Materialising overlapping windows duplicates each input element up to k times. A strided view exposes every window as an alias of the original storage instead.

props.label: route card: next row +5, next column +1

cap.1: Memory is one long street of numbered houses. The shape is a story about it. The route card says how many doors to skip for the next row or column.
cap.2: A 4x5 tensor is 20 numbers in a row. x.stride() is (5, 1): skip 5 elements to go down a row, 1 to go along it. The shape is just how you read the line.
cap.3: Element [i, j] lives at storage_offset + i*s0 + j*s1. A contiguous (4, 5) tensor has strides (5, 1). A transpose only swaps the strides; no data moves.

cap.1: Hand over a new card: 4 stops, skip 6 doors each time. On the 4-by-5 street that walks straight down the diagonal. Not one house moved.
cap.2: as_strided(x, (4,), (6,)) on a 4x5 tensor of 0..19 visits 0, 6, 12, 18: the diagonal. Add them up and you have the trace. It is a view, not a copy.
cap.3: Stride 6 = s0 + s1, so each step moves one row and one column. trace = view.sum(); matmul is built the same way, as a strided view plus a reduction.

cap.1: Give both legs of the route a step of one door. Each row is a window, and neighbours overlap. House 2 shows up three times but exists once.
cap.2: View a length-6 x as size (4, 3), stride (1, 1): four windows of three. Twelve entries, still six numbers in memory. einsum it with the kernel and you have conv1d.
cap.3: The kernel axis reuses the stride of the axis it slides along, so windows alias one storage. With channels, einsum 'b ic ow kw, oc ic kw -> b oc ow' is conv1d.

chapters.name: The literal postman
chapters.verdict: as_strided asks nothing. Read the route, never guess it.

cap.1: The postman follows your card to the letter and never asks if it makes sense. A wrong card gets you the wrong houses, not an error.
cap.2: Compute window strides from x.shape and conv passes every test, then returns garbage on a transposed or sliced input. Use x.stride(), or call .contiguous() first.
cap.3: as_strided ignores the logical shape and indexes storage from storage_offset. After a transpose or step-2 slice, shape-derived strides describe a layout the tensor lacks: wrong reads, no exception.

chapters.name: Why it matters
items: Conv2d = a strided view times a kernel

cap.1: You will rarely write as_strided again. But Conv2d stops being magic: it is a clever route over the same houses, then a sum.
cap.2: ARENA marks this optional. After it, Conv2d is a view plus einsum, a broadcast is a zero stride, a transpose is swapped strides. Use the library ops; know what is inside.
cap.3: Views versus copies comes back when you cache or edit activations inside a model to understand and steer it: always know when two tensors share storage.

coda.title: Hand the postman a route card

readouts.label: sum of what you read
readouts.f: off + (n-1)*st > 19 ? 'not meaningful: you left the tensor' : sum(range(n).map(i => off + i*st))

readouts.label: left the tensor?
readouts.f: off + (n-1)*st > 19 ? 'yes: you are outside the 20 numbers you meant' : 'no, every stop is inside 0..19'

caption.1: Skip 6 from house 0 walks the diagonal; the sum is the trace. Skip 5 walks a column. Skip 0 knocks on one door again and again.
caption.2: The tensor holds 0..19 with stride (5, 1). Stride 5 is a column, 6 the diagonal, 0 repeats one element: that is how a broadcast costs nothing. Watch the (row, col) readout.
caption.3: address(i) = offset + i*stride: a line whose slope is the stride. Stride 0 is expand. Past address 19 you are outside the tensor you meant; the shape is never consulted.

where_else: Conv2d and max-pooling: a sliding-window view, then a weighted sum or a max
Broadcasting and expand: a stretched axis is an axis with stride 0
Transpose and einops patterns: each compiles down to a size and a stride

hamming.what: Setting a tensor's size and stride by hand to get a new view of the same memory, with nothing copied.
hamming.when: Once, in [0.2], to build convolution from a window view and an einsum; later, whenever a view hands you strange numbers.
hamming.why: It turns Conv2d, broadcasting and transpose from magic into different routes over one line of numbers.

object.title: The window rack
object.subtitle: Rows of windows over one strip of houses; each bar's height is the house it points at.

knobs.label: window step (stride of the window axis)

cap.1: Six windows of three houses each. A bar's height is the house number it points at.
cap.2: A (6, 3) window view of one strip. Height = storage address = r*1 + c*1.
cap.3: Height encodes the address r*s_w + c*s_k with both strides 1: the standard sliding window.

cap.1: Look along the slants: equal heights mean the same house, seen by up to three windows. Nothing was copied.
cap.2: Equal heights are shared memory. Overlapping windows alias the same numbers, so the view costs nothing.
cap.3: Cells with equal r + c alias one storage element. That stride aliasing is why the window view is free.

cap.1: Now each window steps three houses. No overlap: every bar is a different house, like cutting the strip into pieces.
cap.2: Window step equal to the kernel size gives non-overlapping windows, the same as reshaping the strip to (6, 3).
cap.3: With s_w = k the view maps one-to-one onto 18 contiguous elements: equivalent to reshape(6, 3), no aliasing.

cap.1: Step zero: every window is the same three houses. That is how one row can be repeated for free.
cap.2: A zero stride repeats data without copying it. That is exactly how broadcasting and expand work.
cap.3: s_w = 0 makes every row alias row 0: expand semantics, a size-6 axis that stores a single copy.

cap.1: Step two: windows overlap by one house. In convolution language, this is a stride-2 convolution.
cap.2: Window step 2 skips every other position. A conv's stride argument is just this stride on the window axis.
cap.3: Conv stride s multiplies the window-axis stride by s; kernel axes keep the input's own stride.

predict.q: Six numbers viewed as four overlapping windows of three shows 12 entries. How many numbers are stored?

options.t: Twelve: each window holds its own copy

predict.why: as_strided only writes a new route. Overlapping windows point at the same storage, so nothing is duplicated.

predict.q: You transpose x, then build windows with strides computed from x.shape. What happens?

options.t: Correct windows: transpose moved the data

predict.why: Transpose swaps strides and leaves memory alone. Shape-based strides now describe the wrong layout, and as_strided never checks.

predict.q: Which stride repeats one element along an axis for free?
predict.why: Stride 0 means 'stay at the same house', which is exactly how broadcasting works.

object.where: Anywhere data is viewed rather than copied: transposes, broadcasts, pooling and convolution windows.
